To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(a) the current epidemiological classification of HIV/AIDS in the United States is not gender neutral, (b) the current epidemiology of HIV/AIDS in women is based on a false premise that heterosexual women are the most vulnerable group, and (c) the current epidemiologic classification of HIV/AIDS is not inclusive of all women and men.

the current surveillance categories allow for the emergence and perpetuation of a discourse of vulnerability concerning heterosexual transmission, while at the same time creating a lack of fathomable risk concerning lesbian and bisexual transmission.
epidemiological classifications are shifting in ways that are both productive and problematic.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the way that gender and sexuality intersect with other social categories to create and maintain social inequalities in the HIV epidemic and in public health.

the way in which the HIV epidemic is understood in terms of gender, sexuality, race, and class, and with the way in that these categories are understood as intersecting and interacting with one another in the construction of the epidemic.
the way in which gender, sexuality, ethnicity, and other social markers intersect with one another to produce and reproduce inequalities in HIV risk.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
epidemiological fathomability is a social process. It is a social process that is informed by the social and political contexts in which it is produced.
the HIV/AIDS epidemic is not fathomable, and that the current epidemiological classifications are not adequate to the task of comprehending the epidemic.
epidemiological classifications are not neutral or value‐free, but rather are infused with assumptions about gender and sexuality that shape the ways in which we understand the epidemic.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the HIV/AIDS epidemic is a gendered epidemic, in which the epidemiological categories that are used to describe the epidemic are gendered.
epidemiological classifications of HIV risk are gendered and sexualized, and that the way they are constructed is important to the way in which HIV prevention is conceptualized and delivered.
the HIV epidemic has become increasingly complex and that the public health discourse of risk and vulnerability has not been able to keep up with this complexity.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the current epidemiological classifications of women's HIV transmission risks are not neutral.
the HIV epidemic is not a gender‐neutral phenomenon.
the current epidemiological classifications and surveillance practices in the United States are insufficient for understanding the complexities of HIV risk and vulnerability.
